questions.q: What does this lesson say is the risk of choosing a custom object when a standard object was actually close enough to the domain entity?
options: There is no real risk -- custom objects are always strictly better
Custom objects cannot be related to any other object
It gives up standard-object benefits for free, such as native integrations, built-in automation, and reporting other teams already expect to find on that object
Custom objects are automatically less secure than standard objects
questions.explain: Choosing custom when a standard object fits well enough forgoes the free built-in benefits (integrations, automation hooks, familiar reporting) that come with the standard object.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what makes the lookup-vs-master-detail decision a lifecycle decision, not just a technical one?
options: Master-detail ties a child record's existence and default sharing to its parent, so deleting the parent affects the children -- the right choice depends on whether the domain model says the child has independent existence or not
Master-detail and lookup are functionally identical in every respect
Lookup relationships are always faster to query than master-detail relationships
This decision has no connection to the domain model at all
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly ties the choice to the domain model's lifecycle: master-detail fits when the child has no independent existence without the parent, lookup fits when the related record has its own independent lifecycle.

questions.q: What example does this lesson give for when master-detail is the right fit?
options: A Claim that references a Technician, where the Technician should survive independently of any one Claim
Two completely unrelated custom objects with no shared data
A relationship between two different Salesforce orgs
A Claim Line Item that only means anything in the context of its parent Claim
questions.explain: A Claim Line Item with no independent existence or meaning apart from its parent Claim is the lesson's example of where master-detail's existence-and-sharing dependency genuinely fits the domain model's lifecycle.

questions.q: Why does this lesson argue security should be designed alongside the data model rather than layered on after?
options: Because security has no real connection to data modeling
Because a gap in who can see or edit records is far more expensive to discover during user acceptance testing than it would be to catch with a five-minute question during data-model mapping
Because Salesforce automatically applies correct sharing rules to every new object without architect involvement
Because security should always be designed before the domain model, not alongside the data model
questions.explain: The lesson's practical argument is that catching a sharing or field-level-security gap during data-model mapping is far cheaper than discovering it later when someone notices they can see records they shouldn't.

questions.q: Why does this lesson avoid re-teaching deep sharing-rule and large-data-volume mechanics in detail?
options: Because those topics are irrelevant to Application Architects
Because Salesforce no longer requires those prerequisite certifications

Because this course assumes the Data Architect and Sharing and Visibility Architect prerequisite knowledge already exists, and instead focuses on how that knowledge gets applied specifically in one application's design
Because sharing rules were deprecated in a recent Salesforce release
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly states it builds on, rather than re-teaches, the prerequisite Data Architect and Sharing and Visibility Architect skill sets, focusing instead on their application within this course's application-design context.
